blocks.0: Cat-O-Fit plans and supports your training{hi} – for you and your whole family. You use it to work towards your goals – a target race or a training programme without a race (fitness, strength, weight loss, mobility): you set up your goal, get a plan for it, train – and watch your progress, step by step.
blocks.1: The app saves every change straight away on your device and syncs it with your own server or NAS – without a connection, simply later, even in the middle of a training session.
blocks.2: You can add the app to your home screen (Share icon in Safari → “Add to Home Screen”). It then launches full-screen like a real app.

blocks.0: Cat-O-Fit keeps planning and doing clearly apart:
1: Goal – a race (e.g. your half marathon) or a training programme without a race.
Training plan – built automatically in phases up to the race, or across the programme’s duration.
Planned sessions – in the calendar, and you can move them.
Completed training – what you actually did (planned vs. actual).
blocks.2: Go to “Today”

anmelden.q: Signing in, switching and signing out
anmelden.aliases: login|log in|sign in|sign out|log out|logout|PIN|password|switch profile|switch user|shared device|shared iPad

blocks.0: The very first time you start, a short wizard sets up the app: first create the admin person with their own PIN (4 to 8 digits, not 0000), then load demo data or start empty. After that, when signed out, Cat-O-Fit shows only the sign-in – the menus appear once you have signed in.
1: Tap your tile and enter your PIN. The server checks it; after five wrong attempts there is a short pause.
There is no separate profile switch: just sign out – you land straight back at the sign-in.
Signing out: on iPhone via “More” (at the top, by your name), on iPad and Mac at the bottom of the sidebar – or in Settings → Account.
blocks.2: Reloading keeps you signed in; only closing the app or the tab signs you out. So on a shared iPad always tap “Sign out” – or switch on “Shared device” in Settings → Account: then signing out clears all personal data from the device.
blocks.3: Without a server connection you can only sign in on a device where you have signed in online before. The app only syncs cycle, labs and supplements once the server has confirmed your sign-in – until then everything stays safely on the device. If the confirmation is missing (for example after an update), the app asks for your PIN once.
blocks.4: The “Team/family” menu item is your shared overview with team badges. Administration (adding members, roles, teams) is under More → “Manage team” and is visible to admins only; “Reset app” is at the very bottom of Settings.

blocks.0: Every trend chart gives you concrete numbers – you don’t have to guess what the curve is showing right now.
1: Run your finger (or, on a computer, the mouse) across the chart.
A guide line jumps to the nearest data point and a small bubble shows the date and value.
With several curves – such as fitness, fatigue and form – you see all three values for the same day at once.
On a computer you can also use the keyboard: move with the arrow keys, close with Escape.
blocks.2: The y-axis shows round reference values with thin grid lines – so you can see the range at a glance, without touching the chart.

belastung-pruefen.q: Checking whether your load is still healthy

blocks.0: The “Load & form” card on “Today” answers three questions – in plain language instead of jargon.
1: Are you building up too fast? The load ratio compares your last 7 days with the average of the three weeks before (ACWR). 1.3 means “30% more than usual”; between 0.8 and 1.3 you are close to your average.
Are you recovered? Fitness minus fatigue gives your form – ranked relative to your fitness: fresh, balanced, in training or clearly tired. Only rated once there are roughly three months of data.
Are you training too uniformly? A note appears only when your training days look very alike and the week is well above your average; walking and mobility don’t count here.
blocks.2: The thresholds are a guide drawn from observational data in team sport – not an injury barometer and not a promise of protection. In the first four weeks the card honestly says “Your data is still building up”. Strength, football and cycling count just like running; the values are load points (AU = minutes × effort).

wettkampf-anlegen.q: Creating a race and generating the plan

0: Open “Goals & plans” and tap “+” → choose “Race”.
Enter the name, date, distance and target time, and choose the priority: A – season highlight, B – important race, C – build-up or fun race.
Save – you land on the goal page.
Tap “Create plan” and choose your level (Beginner, Intermediate, Advanced), run days per week (3–6) and whether you have fixed commitments (e.g. club training) – none by default.

Cat-O-Fit spreads the weeks across the phases Base → Build → Peak → Taper: volume starting from where you are now, at most 8–12% more per week, every 4th week easier, the long run capped, the race session on your race day – whatever the weekday.
blocks.1: Cat-O-Fit derives the target paces from your target time – you don’t have to calculate anything{hi}. If the target time is very ambitious or the preparation is short, the app tells you honestly and suggests alternatives.
blocks.2: Plans already running can be recalculated with the current plan logic via ↻ “Recalculate from today” – everything before today stays as it is.

programm-starten.q: Starting a training programme without a race

blocks.0: You just want to get fitter, stronger or healthier – without a race? Then create a training programme.
1: Open “Goals & plans” and tap “+” → choose “Training programme”.
Choose a focus: General fitness, Strength & muscle, Weight loss or Mobility & health.
Set the training days per week (3–5) and the duration (4, 8 or 12 weeks).
Save & create plan – the weekly plan is ready straight away.
blocks.2: Endurance builds week by week into the WHO range (from 150 minutes, walking counts), plus strength on two days – from getting started to harder variations. Every 4th week is easier. “Recalculate plan from today” creates the coming weeks afresh; anything already done stays.

0: On the dashboard or in the calendar, tap today’s session.
You see the target (distance, target pace, HR zone). Tap “Start”.
In workout mode the clock runs; for intervals Cat-O-Fit guides you with sound through warm-up, effort, rest and cool-down – with the target pace and HR zone of each phase.
At the end tap “End workout” → enter distance, effort (RPE) and feeling → done. Discarding without saving asks you to confirm.
blocks.1: On long runs Cat-O-Fit automatically reminds you to drink. On iPhone: don’t lock the screen (otherwise the signals pause, though the time keeps running correctly) and keep the silent switch off – Safari can’t vibrate.

training-nachtragen.q: Logging a training afterwards, without a watch

blocks.0: You ran without your phone, or forgot it? No problem.
1: Open the session (dashboard, calendar or plan).
Tap “Log as done”.
Enter what you know (distance, time, feeling) – everything is optional.
blocks.2: The planned-vs-actual comparison is honest: an easy run that was far too fast doesn’t count as “Target largely hit”; intervals aren’t judged on the average of the whole session.

training-ohne-plan.q: Logging a training without a plan

blocks.0: A spontaneous bike ride, a run on a rest day or training with no goal at all – that belongs in your training diary too.
1: On “Today” tap “Log activity” – or in the calendar (week view) tap the “+” in the day header.
Enter sport, date, duration, distance, heart rate and effort.
If a planned session on the same day fits, the app offers to link the training to it.
blocks.2: Unplanned activities appear in the calendar, on “Today” and in Progress under “Sessions without a plan” – open, edit or delete them there. “Today” suggests imported activities (Apple Health, GPX/TCX) for matching.

einheit-verschieben.q: Rescheduling a session without wrecking your week
einheit-verschieben.aliases: reschedule|move|postpone|drag and drop|drag & drop|what-if|tomorrow|day after tomorrow|swap days|change date|next free day

blocks.0: Something comes up – that’s normal. What matters is that the week after still adds up.
1: Open the session → “Reschedule”: “Tomorrow”, “Day after tomorrow” or “Next free day” with one tap – or pick a date.
In the calendar (week view) you can also drag: hold the session by its handle (⠿) and drag it to another day.

Cat-O-Fit checks immediately: is something already there? Is there a demanding session (tempo, intervals, strength, long run) the day before or after? Below you see the effect on the weekly load – before and after.
Confirm if it works. The session then carries the note “Moved”; a drag in the calendar can be reversed with “Undo”.
blocks.2: The notes don’t block anything – you reschedule anyway if you want to. The rescheduled session still counts towards the weekly load and the week check.

einheiten-anpassen.q: Adjusting, adding and catching up on sessions

blocks.0: Your plan belongs to you – adjust it whenever you like.
1: Open a session and tap the pencil icon at the top: type, target pace, HR zone, interval structure, distance and description are all editable.

With the “+” in the training plan you create a brand-new session – with a wide choice of sports: swimming, hiking, rowing, tennis, badminton, squash, table tennis, indoor cycling, elliptical, gym training and more.
In the edit dialog you can also delete a session.
blocks.2: If you create a session yourself and a similarly intense one is already in the same week, Cat-O-Fit offers to take that one out of the plan – so the weekly load stays constant. You decide: “Remove from plan” or “Keep both”.
blocks.3: Has something fundamentally changed for a week (e.g. start of the season, a training camp)? In the plan’s “Weeks at a glance” overview, “Recalculate this week” recalculates just that one week afresh – training you have already done is kept.
blocks.4: Missed? Past, open sessions show up as “Overdue”. On the dashboard a note reminds you to reschedule, log or tick them off.
blocks.5: If you have marked a key session (tempo, intervals, long run, strength) as missed, the dashboard offers to make it up on a free day next week – instead of letting it lapse.

koerperwerte.q: Keeping your body stats up to date

0: Tap “＋ Log” → “Body stats” (or Progress → Body → “+”).
Enter e.g. weight, resting heart rate or sleep – only what you want.
The charts show your trend with a y-scale, and for weight with a target line.
“Muscle mass” is the value from a body-analysis scale; “Lean mass” (e.g. from Apple Health) is considerably higher and feeds into energy availability.
HRV method: Apple stores SDNN, many watches and rings show RMSSD. The numbers aren’t comparable – trend, goals and readiness only compare values of the same measurement type.
blocks.1: Want the exact value? Drag your finger across a chart (on a computer: hover with the mouse) – a guide line jumps to the nearest point and shows date + value.
blocks.2: The presentation is deliberately neutral: it’s about the trend, not daily fluctuations. You can hide individual values in Settings.

apple-health.q: Importing Apple Health: automatically or free via file

blocks.0: Your sources (Garmin, Apple Watch, Withings …) write to Apple Health. From there the most important values reach Cat-O-Fit{hi} – weight, resting heart rate, HRV, VO₂max, sleep, steps, active energy and workouts. There are three ways:
1: Automatically with “Health Auto Export – JSON+CSV” (App Store): the app itself is free, but the automatic transfer you need (REST API) is only available with Premium – according to the App Store about €8 a year or €30 one-off. Set-up: in Cat-O-Fit, under Health import, “Switch on auto-import” and copy the endpoint URL; in Health Auto Export, under Automations → + → “REST API”, paste the URL, method POST, format JSON (export version 2), choose metrics + workouts, aggregation “daily”, period “Since last sync” → save → “Run now”.

Free and automatic via a shortcut: with Apple’s “Shortcuts” app you can read health values and send them to the same address – the instructions are in the docs (Apple Health). Whether the automation runs reliably while the iPhone is locked depends on iOS.

Free, by hand: iPhone → Health app → profile picture → “Export All Health Data” and upload the ZIP under Health import (full import). Individual recordings as a GPX or TCX file (Garmin, Strava …) work too – with sport, moving time, kilometre splits and time in HR zones.
blocks.2: You only need an additional login (“Authorization” header) if your instance sits behind an upstream login – the container’s built-in Basic Auth lets the health endpoint through anyway. Check: in Health import, “Recently imported (automatic)” shows the daily values taken over; manual entries are kept, duplicate workouts are detected.

health-connect.q: Android: importing values from Health Connect
health-connect.aliases: Android|Google Fit|Samsung Health|HC Webhook|Pixel Watch|Galaxy Watch|Health Connect|bridge app|import|sync

blocks.0: On Android, Health Connect collects the values from your watch and apps. Websites can’t read from it – so a small bridge app on the device sends the data to Cat-O-Fit, for example the open-source “HC Webhook”.
1: In Cat-O-Fit, under Health import, “Switch on auto-import” and copy the endpoint URL and key.
In the bridge app, enter the URL as the webhook address and send the key as the header “X-Catofit-Token” (if that isn’t possible: append “&token=<key>” to the address).
Allow the data types: weight, body fat, lean body mass, resting heart rate, HRV, sleep, steps, active calories, workouts and heart rate. Cycle only if you want it imported – it stays private.
blocks.2: Cat-O-Fit detects days and workouts that were sent twice. HRV from Health Connect is RMSSD and is evaluated separately from Apple values (SDNN).

kraft-import.q: Bringing your strength history from Strong, Hevy or FitNotes

blocks.0: Logged your strength training in Strong, Hevy or FitNotes? Bring the history along: Cat-O-Fit reads their CSV export and creates a strength session with sets (reps × kg) for every workout.
1: In the other app, export your workout history as a CSV file.
In Cat-O-Fit, open Health import and, under “Strength training from other apps”, tap “Choose CSV file”.
Check the overview – workouts, period, matched exercises. If the file does not say whether the weights are in kg or lb, choose it. Then import.
blocks.2: Exercises the library knows are matched to it; all others keep their own name, so nothing is lost. Rows without repetitions (cardio, timed holds) are skipped, and importing the same file again adds nothing twice.

blocks.0: The most reliable way on iPhone/iPad is the native calendar.
1: Open a session or the plan and tap the export icon.
Choose “Complete plan”, “This session” or “Race only”.
The .ics file opens in the iOS calendar – including a reminder 1 hour before and on the evening before.

blocks.0: Under “Progress” you see at a glance where you stand – right at the top the traffic light “Am I on track?”.
1: Traffic light (green/amber/red): sums up adherence, load and missed sessions over the last 4 weeks – with reasons.
Plan adherence: how many due sessions you completed in the 4-week window.
Weekly volume & training load: your load over time (7 vs. 28 days).
Missed sessions: by reason – those due to injury or illness don’t count against you.
Metrics & goals: weight, circumference, pace, resting heart rate & VO₂max with a trend arrow and “maintain/improve”.
Training year: a heatmap of the last 12 months (like on GitHub) – the darker a day, the more training time.
Race prediction: a rough estimate of your possible time.
blocks.2: Go to Progress

blocks.0: At the bottom (iPhone) or on the left (iPad, Mac): Today · Calendar · ＋ Log · Progress · More. “＋ Log” is the fixed place for training, body stats, meal, lab value, period and checklist item. “Progress” bundles Training (statistics), Body, Badges and Reports as tabs. “More” is organised by topic and shows at the top who is signed in – when you are managing a member, with “Back to me”.

Your start screen for the day: today’s session (the ▶ starts it directly), countdown to the next race, a coach tip (more can be unfolded), load & form, week overview and your weekly and health goals. In landscape orientation on iPad or Mac it uses two columns.
blocks.1: Open

blocks.0: Month and week view of all planned sessions and unplanned activities. In the week view you can reschedule by dragging. Every entry leads to the session.
blocks.1: Open

blocks.0: Your races and training programmes in one place – create, edit, generate a plan. Races with countdown and priority (A – season highlight, B – important, C – build-up), programmes with a focus and training days per week.
blocks.1: Open

blocks.0: The plan for a race or programme: phase timeline, key facts (level, run days, target paces), the “Weeks at a glance” overview and all sessions. Via “…” at the top you update it from today, set fixed commitments or export it to your calendar.

A single session in three states: planned (the target, with “Start · Log as done” at the bottom), in progress (workout mode) and completed (review with a planned-vs-actual comparison; from GPX/TCX also splits and time in HR zones).
Full screen for training: large controls, stopwatch or interval control with target pace and HR zone for each phase, a set counter with rest countdown for strength training, drink-break reminder.

Your body measurements as trends with a Y scale and a target marker – plotted by date, over 3 months, 1 year or everything; long series as weekly averages. Moving a finger or the mouse over the chart shows the date + value. Log, edit, import.
blocks.1: Open

blocks.0: A traffic light “Am I on track?”, plan adherence, weekly volume, training-year heatmap, training load, missed sessions by reason, distribution of sessions, metrics & goals (maintain/improve), race prediction, plus current form and training zones.
blocks.1: Open

blocks.0: Your momentum and all badges with progress – earned ones in colour, open ones with a progress bar.
blocks.1: Open

blocks.0: 93 exercises for strength, core, mobility, cardio and prevention – each one as an animation in the rhythm of the movement, plus step-by-step instructions, muscle groups, equipment, difficulty, tip, progression and a caution note. They include Hyrox exercises such as wall balls and kettlebell swings, back and hip stretches, and prevention exercises for running and football (Nordic hamstring, Copenhagen, FIFA 11+ warm-up). Football sessions suggest them directly.
1: Filter by category at the top (strength/core/mobility/cardio) AND by body region (back, hips, abs, legs, upper body) – or search in the text field.
Tap an exercise: the figure shows the movement in the rhythm of the exercise, with the working muscles highlighted in colour.

Set the repetitions (seconds for holds) and sets, then tap “Follow along”: the animation counts sets and reps, shows the technique cue and breathing, keeps the rests and shows when to switch sides. “Slow” helps you learn, “Sound” gives an audible beat.
At the end the exercise counts as done – or you count up in detail with “Done (+1)”. A completed training session also counts its exercises automatically.

In strength and mobility/recovery sessions, the exercises from the description are listed first (“in your plan”), followed by suggestions based on how often you use them. Tap “+” to add an exercise to the session.
blocks.2: The animations are deliberately schematic and do not replace individual instruction.

durchgehend.q: Follow along non-stop – with music and voice cues

blocks.0: A whole session in one go – like a video to follow along with: the on-screen instructor demonstrates each exercise to the beat, with a break in between showing a preview, side changes and a rest between rounds. Meant for an iPad or phone on the floor; you don’t have to tap anything.
1: Start: in a strength or mobility session, tap “Follow along non-stop” – the amounts come from the description (“12×”, “30 s/side”, “3 rounds”) – or, in the Exercise library under “Workouts”, pick one from the catalogue (search and filters for strength, core, mobility, cardio, running & football).
On the overview, set the rounds and rest, choose music and voice cues, then tap “Let’s go”.
Music: a beat that fits the exercise, every movement on the beat; quieter during breaks. “Own music” lets e.g. Spotify keep playing – for that the device must not be on silent.

Voice cues come during the breaks (next exercise, switching sides). During the exercise, tones guide you: three tones before you start, the last three reps or seconds tick, a double tone at “10 seconds left”, a low tone at the end.
Tapping shows the control bar: pause, back, forward, music and voice cues on/off, finish. Tapping the section bar jumps to that section.
At the end all exercises count as done; from a planned session, “Log as done” records them straight away with the duration.
blocks.2: No sound? Turn the volume up. With “Music” you hear it even when the device is on silent; with “Own music” you don’t.

laborwerte-woher.q: Where do I get my lab results?

blocks.0: In Germany several routes lead to a lab report – they differ mainly in who pays and how sport-specific the choice of values is.
blocks.3: For comparing results over time, stick to the same lab and method where possible. Blood from a fingertip is more sensitive to preparation than a venous blood draw; small jumps between two providers are often measurement differences and not a real change.

referenzbereich.q: Why do I enter my lab’s reference range?

blocks.0: Because in Germany there are NO nationwide uniform reference ranges: every lab sets its own – depending on the measurement method, instrument and comparison group. For ferritin, fT3 or vitamin B12 they differ noticeably. That is why the range is always printed next to the value on your report.
1: When you log a value, the “Your lab’s reference range” fields show a typical range only as a grey hint – in the unit you have chosen.
Copy the range from your report. Only what you enter yourself is saved; if you leave it empty, the typical range applies.
Cat-O-Fit then rates the value against YOUR lab. The sport target range remains alongside it as a second layer.
blocks.2: Up to v3.19.0 the pre-filled default was saved along with the value (and converted incorrectly when you changed the unit). The app recognises such older values and rates them against the typical range again – you don’t need to correct anything.
blocks.3: What is standardised – and what isn’t:

blocks.0: Log values from your lab report, follow their progress and have them put into a sport context. The point: lab ranges apply to the general population – a ferritin of 25 µg/l is “normal”, but marginal for endurance training. Cat-O-Fit shows you both ranges.
1: The first time you open it, you get a few short questions to define the scope – they apply to the whole app: Cat-O-Fit is designed for healthy adults. With illness, medication, pregnancy, breastfeeding or an eating disorder, the module stays at pure documentation, without recommendations. The app recognises children and teenagers from the year of birth: their values are only documented, not rated.

“+ Log a value”: analyte, date, measured value and the unit right next to it – for almost every value the units customary in Germany are available (e.g. CRP in mg/l or mg/dl, vitamin D in nmol/l or ng/ml); the app converts and shows the value as it was on the report. If a value is far outside the usual range, it asks: “Is the unit right?”
Magnesium comes as a whole-blood and as a serum value – please choose the matching one. For B12 there are holo-TC and total B12.

Under “Circumstances of the blood draw” you can note hard exercise in the 48 hours before, fasting, biotin and, for women, the cycle day. After hard exercise the app then does not rate CK, urea and CRP, and rates oestradiol only against your lab’s range for the cycle phase.
Tapping a value shows its progress with both ranges (reference dashed, sport target range as an area), the source of the ranges and all measurements – you can edit and delete values there.

The app shows a trend only from three measurements over at least two months and when the change is larger than the value’s natural variation. A projection (“when will the value leave the favourable range”) exists only in the unfavourable direction and at most one year ahead.
Ferritin is interpreted together with the CRP from the same blood draw: with inflammation a high value cannot be assessed, but a low one is still noteworthy.
Older values (vitamin D after four months or from a different season, most others after a year) stay in the history but no longer carry suggestions – the app then advises a new measurement.

Under “Supplements” you find general information with the reasoning, the usual amount (in line with the BfR maximum levels and the EFSA upper limits), timing and interactions – always the route via food first. A value that is too high never leads to “supplement”, but to the advice to check your intake. For performance products there is a note about batch-tested products (Cologne List).
What you take regularly, you enter under “Your plan” and tick off. Products you only take as needed (e.g. caffeine before races) you mark as such – they don’t count towards adherence.
blocks.2: At the very top the app estimates your energy supply: whether you eat enough for what you train. The calculation uses only days you have confirmed with “Mark day complete” in Nutrition, and the result is a range, not a measurement. For this the app needs your fat-free mass – measured (scales, Apple Health) or from a body-fat value from the last four months. Too little energy is a more common problem in endurance sport than a missing supplement – and a frequent cause of declining performance, injuries and cycle disturbances.
blocks.3: Iron is never suggested without a lab value – taken on suspicion it is harmful when stores are full. Cat-O-Fit is for documentation and general information for healthy adults – not a medical device, not a diagnosis: for abnormal values the app explicitly refers you to a doctor. Your values are private: not visible to admins in the app, and the server only releases them after you sign in with your PIN. However, whoever runs the server can read the stored files.

energieverfuegbarkeit.aliases: RED-S|energy availability|EA|LEA|low energy availability|fat-free mass|lean mass|undereating|not eating enough|energy deficit

blocks.0: Energy supply estimates whether you eat enough for what you train. Technically it is called energy availability: the energy you eat minus exercise energy expenditure, divided by fat-free mass in kg.
1: The calculation uses only days you have confirmed with “Mark day complete” in Nutrition – until enough days are in, the app says so instead of claiming a shortfall.
Guideline about 45 kcal per kg of fat-free mass. With a weight-loss goal, 30–45 is acceptable temporarily; below 30 (for men below 25) it becomes critical for hormones, bones and recovery.
Fat-free mass comes from a measurement (scales, Apple Health) or from a body-fat value from the last four months. Because all inputs are estimates, the app shows a range.
blocks.2: Persistently too little energy is called RED-S (relative energy deficiency in sport) in sports medicine. Cat-O-Fit does not make a diagnosis – with cycle disturbances, frequent injuries or persistent tiredness, this belongs in medical hands.

trendprojektion.q: Trend and projection for lab values

0: A trend appears only from three measurements over at least two months – and only if the change is larger than the value’s natural variation (about ferritin 48 %, vitamin D 30 %, haemoglobin 9 %, otherwise 25 %).
The projection extends the course in a straight line and says when the favourable range would be left – only in the unfavourable direction and at most one year ahead.
Vitamin D varies with the season: a summer value says little in winter.
blocks.1: A projection is a reason for the next check, not a prediction.

blocks.0: Create unalterable records of your progress: a monthly report, a race report (preparation + result) or a certificate for a goal you reached. Before saving you see a preview; once saved, they are kept and can be printed or saved as a PDF – all done locally.
blocks.1: Open

blocks.0: Protein-rich meal ideas with recipe suggestions, a calorie balance for today, an automatic shopping list with pantry stock (from the weekly meal plan) and “Checklist” with reminders: daily routines or appointments with date/time. Appointments also appear automatically in the Calendar (week and month view) and can additionally be exported as .ics – plus templates such as race preparation. Can be switched off in Settings.
Profile, heart rate zones, pace ranges, theme & accent colour, modules, visible values, and “Data & backup” (personal backup for everyone, full family backup & restore for admins).
blocks.1: Open

blocks.0: A good plan builds up in phases – that is easy on you and builds fitness at the same time:
1: Base: lots of easy volume, aerobic base.
Build: threshold runs, speed endurance.
Peak: short, fast stimuli (VO₂max) and race pace.
Taper: volume down, keep the sharpness – fresh on the start line.

blocks.0: Cat-O-Fit uses five zones, derived from your maximum heart rate – optionally with resting heart rate via heart rate reserve (Karvonen) or from your threshold HR (“Threshold”): from performance testing or a 30-minute field test (average HR of the last 20 minutes), zones after Friel. If you don’t know your max HR, the app estimates it in Settings from your age (Tanaka: 208 − 0.7 × age); a measured value is always better.
1: Z1 Recovery – very easy.
Z2 Base endurance – “conversational” pace, this is where endurance is built.
Z3 Steady tempo – brisk, but controlled.
Z4 Threshold – fast, “comfortably hard”.
Z5 VO₂max – very hard, only briefly.
blocks.2: You can adjust max HR and resting heart rate in Settings – the zones are recalculated.

blocks.0: Every session type has a pace range in min/km, derived from your target time. They are a suggestion, not a must – how you feel on the day counts.

rpe.q: RPE – how hard did it feel?
rpe.aliases: effort|exertion|perceived exertion|rate of perceived exertion|Borg|how hard

blocks.0: RPE (1–10) is your subjective perceived exertion. It complements heart rate and pace – especially on days when the numbers “feel different”.
1: 1–2 very light to light – walking, an easy cool-down.
3–4 easy to moderate – you could chat the whole time.
5–6 somewhat hard to challenging – you can still speak in short sentences.
7–8 hard to very hard – tempo, intervals, racing over longer distances.
9–10 extremely hard to maximal – sustainable only briefly, a finishing sprint.
blocks.2: Multiplied by the duration, the effort gives your load points (minutes × RPE).

blocks.0: The statistics show your running kilometres for the last 7 and 28 days – runs only; cycling, walking and swimming don’t count there. If the load rises very quickly, deliberately plan recovery. Cat-O-Fit makes no promises about injury protection, only gives pointers.
blocks.1: The “Load points · 7 days” figure calculates minutes × effort across all sports – so strength, football, cycling or a practice match count too, not just the running km. Without a logged duration the planned duration counts, and only then 30 minutes.
blocks.2: The coach adapts in both directions: if your sessions have been very hard for weeks, the dashboard suggests a lighter week (volume down, fixed dates stay); if they were rather easy and nothing speaks against it, you can step up the coming week a little.

vdot.q: Current form & target paces (VDOT) – how to use them

blocks.0: On Today, the “Current form” card estimates a VDOT (a form/performance figure after Jack Daniels) from your recent running performances and derives suitable training zones from it. Right above it is the “Your training zones” card with the current plan target paces – so you can compare the two directly.
blocks.1: How to read the card:
2: The VDOT chip (e.g. “VDOT 41.9”) is your estimated current performance.

“smoothed over 7 weeks · latest 8.0 km in 38:00 on Wed 1 Jul” means: the form is NOT a single run but a smoothed value from your last weeks – each week your best hard run counts (race, tempo, intervals or an effort of 7 or more), more recent weeks count more, and individual outliers are capped. “latest …” names your most recent quality run. Easy runs underestimate your form – if you only run easy, the card says so and does not advise slower paces.
So the form does NOT jump after a single very fast (or slow) day – it reflects your stable trend.
Easy / Threshold / Intervals are the paces that match this form.
The line below compares form and plan, e.g. “Your form is about 7 s/km faster than your planned target paces – time to sharpen them.” If the two match, it says “suit your current form well”.
4: Tap “Adjust training zones to your form”.

Cat-O-Fit immediately applies the form paces to your training zones AND to all open, future running sessions in your plan – each session gets the zone for its type (long run → long run, threshold → threshold). With a target time, race pace remains your goal.
Afterwards the card says “suit … well” – form and plan match again.
blocks.5: A single outlier day doesn’t shift the form – it is smoothed over several weeks. It does not replace performance testing: if you have determined your maximum heart rate there, enter it in Settings.

trinkpausen.q: Drink breaks on the long run

blocks.0: On long runs, workout mode shows a drink reminder at regular intervals (with a sound, and vibration where possible) – so you don’t forget to drink over long distances. Tip: small sips often rather than a lot rarely.
blocks.1: You can set the interval for each session yourself: in the edit dialog under “Drink break every (min)”. Empty = automatic per type, 0 = off.

coach.q: What does the coach show me?

blocks.0: The coach gives you exactly one recommendation on Today{hi} – in a fixed order, so two cards never contradict each other:
1: Warning signs first: a gentle comeback after illness/injury, a recovery day when the load is clearly higher than planned, easier today when readiness is low, easier after football when the match was hard-played, a lighter week after weeks of very hard sessions.

Then your plan: spread out the day (two sessions on the same day), make up the key session you missed, balance weekly volume (gently making up running km that were left over) – never after illness or injury.
Last, progression (“More in the tank”) – only without a warning sign, with load in the usual range and not in the 14 days after a lay-off.
Below that, information without a verdict of its own: readiness (HRV, resting heart rate, sleep), form forecast, heart rate on easy runs, effort of recent sessions (average RPE).
blocks.2: “Why this recommendation?” below the card shows what else would have fitted. Training according to plan is not a warning sign, and the coach never touches fixed dates. Changes to the plan only happen when you trigger them.

blocks.0: The “Load & form” card on Today summarises your training load – across all sports (running, strength, football …), calculated as load points (AU): minutes × effort (RPE 1–10).
1: Load ratio (ACWR) – your last 7 days in relation to the average of the 21 days before (decoupled: the acute days are not included in their own reference value). 0.8–1.3 means: close to your average.

Fitness / fatigue / form – long-term fitness (CTL) minus short-term fatigue (ATL) gives your form (TSB), classified relative to fitness: fresh (above +10 %), balanced, in training (down to −30 %), clearly tired. During the first roughly three months the fitness curve is still settling in – until then there is no rating.
Monotony & strain – a notice only when uniform training days coincide with a week clearly above your average; very light activity doesn’t count.
blocks.2: Limits of the metric: the values 0.8/1.3/1.5 come from observational data in team sports. That training according to this traffic light prevents injuries is not proven – take it as a pointer to how much your load has risen compared with your own average. These values also feed the automatic recovery day.

blocks.0: Cat-O-Fit measures the load of all sports with one number: load points (AU) = duration in minutes × effort (RPE 1–10). The method is called session RPE and comes from Carl Foster.
1: Example: 45 minutes easy (RPE 4) give 180 points, 60 minutes of intervals (RPE 8) give 480 points.
If the duration is missing, the app works it out from the distance (per sport), then from the planned duration, and finally uses 30 minutes.

If the effort is missing, the app estimates it from your average heart rate relative to your max HR (Settings → “Heart rate zones”) – for intervals, tempo and races never below the typical value, because the rests pull the average down. Without heart rate it uses a typical value for the type of session.
For imported workouts without an effort rating, Today briefly asks (“How hard was it?”) – your own sense is more accurate than any estimate.
blocks.2: Load ratio (ACWR), fitness/fatigue/form and monotony all come from load points – every load judgement has the same source.

blocks.0: Monotony describes how uniform your training days are: the weekly average of the load points divided by their variation (after Foster). Strain is the weekly load times monotony.
1: A notice appears only when both coincide: monotony of 2 or more AND a week at least 10 % above your usual weekly load.
Very light activity (effort up to 3, such as walking or mobility) doesn’t count here.
blocks.2: Variety of hard and easy days lowers monotony – a real rest day has more effect than another easy session.

bereitschaft.q: Readiness: resting heart rate, HRV and sleep
bereitschaft.aliases: readiness|recovery|HRV|heart rate variability|resting heart rate|resting pulse|RHR|sleep|rested|tired

blocks.0: Readiness (0–100) compares your most recent recovery figures with your own normal range: a resting heart rate above your average lowers it, a good seven hours of sleep or more helps, and anything under six and a half hours costs you. For HRV it isn’t a single day that counts but the average of the last seven days compared with the four weeks before – if it sits below that, readiness drops; one bad morning doesn’t tip anything.
1: 75 and above: high · 55–74: solid · 40–54: moderate · below that: low.
HRV counts from three readings in seven days and ten in four weeks – and only within one type of measurement (SDNN or RMSSD).
If the latest readings are more than four days old, the app shows no readiness.
blocks.2: When readiness is low, the coach suggests training more easily today – a recommendation, not a diagnosis.

blocks.0: You enter recurring fixed commitments once – the training plan then arranges itself around them. New plans have no default commitments; the app asks about them when you create one. If the same commitment is in two plans, it only appears once per day.
1: Choose your football training days (e.g. Mon & Wed) and give the duration and intensity (light/normal/intense).
Add recurring matches with a start date (e.g. “from 19 Aug, every Sunday, 2 h”) – they count as hard load.
On a match day the planned session drops out; the week is planned around the fixed commitments.
blocks.2: Football is HIIT-like and costs a lot of energy: from “normal” upwards, a football day counts as a demanding day (it feeds fully into load & form). The plan never puts a quality session or long run directly next to a demanding commitment – if there is no quiet day, the quality session becomes “Easy with strides”. If you played hard and a tough session is still coming up afterwards, the coach suggests taking it more easily.

blocks.0: Cat-O-Fit plans on a rolling basis: instead of a rigid block, the coming week adapts to what you have actually done.
1: If your load is well above what was planned, or hard days pile up that weren’t in the plan, the coach suggests a recovery day for the next hard session in the coming two days. Training that follows the plan is not a warning sign.
If two sessions fall on that day (say from two goals), the whole day is turned down to easy – or you move one to a free day (spread out the day).
If you enter a period start for today or tomorrow, the app asks whether you’d like to take it easier – only then is anything adjusted.
Every automatic adjustment appears transparently in the “Recent automatic adjustments” log and can be undone as long as the session is still open.
blocks.2: Nothing changes behind your back – adjustments are visible and reversible. “Today” only ever shows one recommendation; “Why this recommendation?” shows what was set aside.

blocks.0: The week check in the plan shows when too much overlaps in a week – and the order in which Cat-O-Fit triages.
1: Fixed commitments (football/matches) come first.
Then the key runs (tempo/intervals, long run).
After that strength, and finally extra volume.
Preview (what-if): before you add or move a session, the app shows the effect on the weekly load.

ziel-cockpit.q: Goal cockpit: half marathon + weight loss together

blocks.0: Two goals at once? The goal cockpit brings a performance goal (e.g. a half marathon) and weight loss together at a glance.
1: The emphasis moves with the training phase: in the base phase the deficit is largest (around 450 kcal), in the build phase smaller (around 300 kcal), in the peak phase small and during tapering zero – then you top up.

The deficit recommendation is tied to your calorie balance – with lower limits: never below your basal metabolic rate and never so low that less than 30 kcal per kg of fat-free mass is left after training. Without a body-fat value the deficit is capped at 15%.
An honest stimulus check warns you if too little training stimulus is set for progress.
blocks.2: That’s how you lose weight without ruining the key sessions.

gesundheitsziel.q: How do I set a health goal?

blocks.0: Besides the weekly goals (active minutes & training days), you can set dedicated target values for body stats.
1: Settings → Health goals → “+ Goal”.
Choose a metric (weight, body fat, resting heart rate, HRV or VO₂max), then enter a target value and optionally a target date.
Your current value is remembered as the starting point; progress counts from there towards the goal.
On “Today” the “Health goals” card appears with a progress bar for each goal.
blocks.2: Progress updates with every new body stat (＋ Log → Body stats) or via the Apple Health import.

blocks.0: You unlock badges for completed training and goals reached – automatically, with a little celebration.
blocks.1: Momentum is your “flame of drive”: it grows when you keep going and shrinks gently when there are gaps. It is meant as a nudge, never as a punishment.
2: Streaks count in weeks: a calendar week with at least three training days continues the streak – rest days are part of it.
Momentum rises with up to five training days per week; more doesn’t bring any extra momentum.
Ill or injured? Log the absence with a reason – momentum pauses and the streak doesn’t break.

vorlieben.q: How does Cat-O-Fit learn my preferences?

blocks.0: In Nutrition you mark favourite dishes with ♥ and tap “Cooked” after cooking. From that, Cat-O-Fit learns which tags (e.g. high-protein, vegetarian) you prefer and suggests matching dishes under “Recommended for you”.
blocks.1: The daily checklist also remembers what you use often and offers it as a quick add.

kalorienbilanz.q: How does the calorie balance work?

blocks.0: At the top of Nutrition you see your daily balance: energy used versus energy taken in.
1: Used = basal metabolic rate (from height, weight, year of birth, sex) + everyday activity + today’s training.
Taken in = the entries in your food diary for today. “Cooked” and “Log what you ate” write into it; “Eaten today” lists them (each can be deleted individually).

The daily target is based on your target weight (lose/maintain/gain) – calculated with the weekly average of your scale, not a single measurement. Within 0.5 kg of the target counts as “maintain”; if you drop below a weight-loss target you get “maintain”, never automatically “gain”.
When losing weight, the daily target stays above your basal metabolic rate and above your training needs. If your target weight is below a BMI of 18.5, the app calculates no deficit.
Once you have logged everything for the day, tap “Mark day complete” under “Eaten today” – only such days count towards energy availability in the labs module.
blocks.2: When you create a meal, the “estimate” button roughly estimates the kcal from the ingredients. Everything is meant as a guide – not diet advice.
blocks.3: For the balance you need height, weight and year of birth in your profile; sex makes the basal metabolic rate more accurate.

eignung.q: Scope and limits, child and youth profile and “Hide calorie figures”

blocks.0: Cat-O-Fit is for documentation and general information for healthy adults – it is not a medical device. A short scope check (Settings → Health & suitability) applies to the whole app:
1: Illness or medication: labs and supplements for documentation only, with no recommendations.
Pregnancy, breastfeeding or an eating disorder: in addition, no weight-loss or deficit goals and no weight-loss programme.
Under 18 (from the year of birth): child and youth profile – no calorie or weight goals, no weight-loss programme, no performance supplements, lab values documented only, calorie figures hidden.
“Hide calorie figures” hides kcal figures in Nutrition, on “Today” and in energy availability – for anyone who doesn’t feel good about numbers around eating.
blocks.2: Until the scope check has been answered, the app suggests no weight-loss deficit. The questions are deliberately not pre-filled.

einkaufsliste.q: How does the shopping list work?

blocks.0: The shopping list is shared and is built automatically from the meal plans of all members:
1: Each member plans dishes with portions for the week in Nutrition (basket icon).
Cat-O-Fit pulls all the planned dishes together, adds up the ingredients (e.g. oats from several people into one amount) and subtracts the shared pantry – the list shows exactly what you need.
When you shop, tap “Bought everything → add to pantry”: the amounts move into the shared pantry. “Cooked” deducts them again.
blocks.2: The shopping day applies to everyone and is set by admins in the team/family management (default Tuesday).

wetter.q: How do I use the weather in the plan?

0: Open Settings → “Location & weather” and search for your city.
In the calendar, small weather icons with the temperature appear for the next few days.
In heat, rain or storms, the session concerned shows a suitable note.
blocks.1: Weather data comes from Open-Meteo. Without internet the last loaded data stays in place – the app carries on as normal.

zyklus.q: What does the cycle calendar do?

blocks.0: Log your period start (“＋ Log” → “Period”, or on the cycle page). From that, Cat-O-Fit calculates your cycle length, the current phase (menstruation/follicular/ovulation/luteal) and the forecast for your next period. If you don’t need the cycle, switch the module off under Settings → Modules.
blocks.1: On your menstruation days, sessions are “protected”: you can move or skip them without judgement – they don’t count as missed and reduce neither plan adherence nor momentum. The phase tips are deliberately neutral: the research on performance differences across the cycle is weak – how you feel is what counts.
blocks.2: With hormonal contraception (the pill, hormonal coil, implant …) there are no natural phases: with the switch on the cycle page, Cat-O-Fit only shows your bleeding days. With no new entry for about three months, the forecast pauses.
blocks.3: Sensitive data stays local on your own server – the module can be switched off at any time.

blocks.0: Yes. Cat-O-Fit saves every change locally straight away and syncs in the background as soon as there is a connection again – ideal for training on the go.

datenschutz.q: Is my data safe? What is stored where?

0: On your device: a copy of your data so the app works offline. With “Shared device” (Settings → Account), signing out clears it away again.
On your server: all data for all people as files in the “data” folder – that is also the complete backup.
To the outside: only the weather request and – if switched on – the nutrition lookup (see below). No account, no ads, no tracking.
blocks.1: Your data lives as files on your own server or NAS, not in someone else’s cloud. The server only hands out cycle, labs and supplements after your PIN sign-in – not even to admins. All other data (training, plans, body stats) can be read by any device that can reach your server; the app therefore belongs on your own home network (from outside only with a sign-in in front of it). Whoever runs the server can read all the files.
blocks.2: Only two extra services that can be switched off reach the outside: the weather request to Open-Meteo (from the device, with place or coordinates) and – if switched on – the nutrition lookup at Open Food Facts (from the server, with the ingredient name only).
blocks.3: Under Settings → “Data & backup” you can export your personal backup at any time (including cycle, labs and supplements). Admins can additionally back up a full family backup of all members and restore it in an emergency – for privacy reasons without the private areas.

blocks.0: Yes! Cat-O-Fit is for your whole team or family (up to 32 people). At start-up the sign-in appears – tap your tile and enter your PIN.
blocks.1: Each member has their own plans, training, body stats and settings.
blocks.2: Admins manage the team or family (More → “Manage team”: add members, roles, teams, shopping day) and can “Open” a member, e.g. to plan for children or the team – the top of the screen then reads “You are managing …” with “Back to me”. Cycle, labs and supplements always stay private in the process. Adding members, changing roles and removing them only work with a connection to the server.
blocks.3: In Settings → Visibility on the team/family dashboard you decide whether your main goal and your figures are shown – hidden goals appear on the dashboard as “🔒 private”.
blocks.4: Newly added members start with the PIN “0000”; until they set their own in Settings → Account (using the previous PIN), “Today” reminds them. Forgotten your PIN? An admin opens the member and sets a new one under Settings → Account. If the only admin has forgotten their PIN, the only help is working on the server itself (see Troubleshooting).

teams.q: Forming teams, assigning members and evaluating per team

blocks.0: Besides the whole family, as an admin you can form teams – e.g. “Team Red”, “Team Blue”, “Team Green”. A member can be in SEVERAL teams at once, and some stay without any team at all.
blocks.1: You create teams under More → “Manage team”: “Create team”, choose a name and icon and assign the members with ticks. To change teams, simply move the ticks – that’s how you take someone out of one team and put them into another (or additionally into a second).
blocks.2: On the team/family dashboard you switch at the top between “All”, the individual teams and “No team”. All figures – weekly kilometres, monthly km & milestone, “Active this week” and the team badges – are then added up for exactly the members of the chosen team.
blocks.3: A member in two teams counts in both – handy if someone is, say, in the running group AND the football team.
blocks.4: If a member is removed, they disappear automatically from all teams – no “ghosts” are left behind.

blocks.0: In-app notices only work while the app is open. For reliable reminders, export the session to the iOS calendar (.ics) – the reminder it contains also works when the app is closed.

kalender-abo.q: Subscribe to the plan in your calendar

blocks.0: Instead of opening individual .ics files, your calendar can subscribe to an entire plan – all sessions and the race. It then fetches changes by itself. What you subscribe to is always a plan, not the app’s calendar.
1: More → “Goals & plans” → open a race or programme → tap the download icon “Export” at the top – or in the plan “…” → “Add to calendar (.ics)”.
In the “Export to calendar” window, tap “Copy subscription link”. The button only appears with a connection to the server and after your PIN sign-in.
Paste the link into your calendar as a subscription:
blocks.2: iPhone/iPad: Calendar app → “Calendars” → “Add Calendar” → “Add Subscription Calendar”.
blocks.4: Google: in a browser on a computer, click + next to “Other calendars” → “From URL” (this isn’t possible in the Google app).
blocks.6: Only reachable on your home network? iCloud, Google and Outlook fetch subscriptions over the internet – they can’t subscribe to a server they can’t reach. In that case set the subscription up directly on the device: on the iPhone via iOS Settings → Apps → Calendar → Calendar Accounts → Add Account → Other → “Add Subscribed Calendar”, on the Mac with “Location: On My Mac”. If a sign-in is placed in front (Basic Auth), on the iPhone you enter the username and password there; Google and Outlook can’t do that.
blocks.7: The link points to the server you copy it from and contains your personal calendar key – everyone gets their own. Anyone who knows the link can read the appointments: share it only with people who are allowed to see your plan.
blocks.8: Calendars poll subscriptions on their own schedule; with Outlook a change can take over 24 hours, according to Microsoft. Links from versions before 3.20.0 (without a key) remain valid until 30 November 2026 – after that, set the subscription up again once.

blocks.0: Under Settings → Modules you hide areas you don’t need. All modules are on to begin with. When one is switched off, its menu item and its entry under “＋ Log” disappear; your data is kept.
1: Nutrition – recipes, meal plan, food diary and calorie balance.
Shopping list – shared shopping list and pantry.
Daily checklist – checklist & reminders, including their dates in the calendar.
Cycle calendar – cycle, phases in the calendar and the question on the first day of a period.
Labs & supplements – lab values, energy availability and supplements, including the notes about them in Nutrition.
blocks.2: The switches apply per person. When you manage a member, cycle and labs stay hidden anyway – they are private.

0: The server’s “data” folder is the complete backup – all people, including cycle, labs and supplements. It belongs in the regular backup of the server (e.g. Hyper Backup on the Synology).
Full family backup (admins only, Settings → Data & backup): all members, roles, teams, reports and training data – without the private areas.
My backup (everyone): your own data including cycle, labs and supplements. On iPhone and iPad via the Share menu (“Save to Files”).
blocks.1: The tried-and-tested 3-2-1 rule: three copies, on two different media, one of them off-site. The full backup doesn’t replace backing up the server folder – otherwise, after losing the server, the private areas of everyone without their own backup would be missing.
blocks.2: Go to “Data & backup”

0: New version doesn’t appear: close the app completely (iPhone: swipe up from the bottom edge and flick it away) and reopen it. The app fetches updates when it opens and when it comes back to the foreground.

Status stays “Offline”: is the server reachable on your home network (Wi-Fi, VPN)? Changes stay on the device and go out automatically as soon as the server answers – nothing is lost. “Sync now” in Settings → Data & backup triggers it by hand.

“Please confirm your PIN”: the sign-in to the server has expired or is needed again after an update. With your PIN, cycle, labs and supplements are synced again; “Later” postpones it until the next time you open the app.
Forgotten PIN: an admin opens the member and sets a new PIN under Settings → Account. For the only admin there is a tool for running the server (docs “Troubleshooting”).

“The app could not start”: usually the server doesn’t deliver a file, or delivers it with the wrong file type (for instance after an incomplete update). The message names the file concerned; the operations docs explain the causes.
Health import reports an error: 401 means wrong key, 403 missing key – copy the key again in Health import.
ACWR (load ratio) – load of the last 7 days relative to the average of the 21 days before.
Badges – awards for training and goals reached (Progress → Badges).
Energy availability (RED-S) – what is left of the energy you ate after training, per kg of fat-free mass.
Fat-free mass (FFM, lean body mass) – body weight without fat; measured or calculated from the body-fat value.
Fitness, fatigue, form (CTL, ATL, TSB) – long-term and short-term load and the difference between them.
Goal – a race or a training programme; each with its own plan.
HR zones (Z1–Z5) – heart-rate ranges from recovery to VO₂max.
HRV – heart rate variability; measured as SDNN (Apple) or RMSSD (many watches) – not comparable with each other.
Load points (AU, sRPE) – minutes × effort; the common unit behind all load judgements.
Long run – the long, easy run of the week.
Momentum – your drive from the last few weeks; pauses during illness.
Planned vs actual – comparison of the plan with the training you actually did.
Readiness – daily score from resting heart rate, HRV and sleep compared with your last two weeks.
RPE (effort) – how hard a session was, from 1 (very light) to 10 (maximal).
Session – a planned training in the plan; training – what you actually did.
Tapering – the weeks before a race with less volume so you start fresh.
VDOT – fitness value after Jack Daniels; forecast and training paces come from it.
